sections.title: Virtualization Fundamentals
sections.content:
WHAT VIRTUALIZATION IS.
Virtualization allows multiple operating systems to run simultaneously on a single physical machine. The physical machine â€” the host â€” provides the hardware. Each operating system running on top of the host is a virtual machine â€” also called a guest OS. The guest OS does not run directly on hardware. Instead, the hypervisor intercepts its hardware access requests and fulfills them from the physical resource pool.
From the guest OS's perspective, it appears to have exclusive access to its own CPU, RAM, storage, and network interface. All of these are emulated or virtualized by the hypervisor. The guest cannot tell it is sharing a physical host with other guest systems.
THE HYPERVISOR.
The hypervisor is the software that creates, manages, and isolates virtual machines. It allocates physical CPU time, RAM, and storage to each VM according to configured limits, mediates all hardware access, and enforces isolation between guests.
Two types of hypervisors are distinguished by where they sit in the system stack.
TYPE 1 â€” BARE-METAL HYPERVISOR.
A Type 1 hypervisor installs directly on the physical hardware â€” there is no host operating system underneath it. The hypervisor itself is the system software that the hardware boots into. VMs run on top of the hypervisor.
Type 1 characteristics:
Direct hardware access â€” no host OS consuming resources between the hypervisor and the hardware.
Lower overhead â€” more physical resources available for VMs.
Better performance â€” appropriate for production workloads.
Used in enterprise data centers, server consolidation, and cloud infrastructure.
Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V Server, KVM, Xen, Citrix Hypervisor.
TYPE 2 â€” HOSTED HYPERVISOR.
A Type 2 hypervisor is an application that runs on top of an existing host operating system. The host OS boots first and runs normally. The hypervisor is installed and launched like any other application. VMs run within the hypervisor's environment, which is itself running within the host OS.
Type 2 characteristics:
Easier to install â€” installs on any workstation with a supported OS.
More overhead â€” the host OS consumes CPU and RAM before the hypervisor even starts.
Lower performance â€” appropriate for development, testing, training, and personal lab use.
Examples: VMware Workstation, Oracle VirtualBox, Parallels Desktop, Microsoft Virtual PC.
CPU REQUIREMENTS.
Hardware virtualization extensions must be present and enabled. Intel CPUs use VT-x â€” Intel Virtualization Technology for IA-32/64. AMD CPUs use AMD-V â€” AMD Virtualization. These extensions allow the CPU to run guest code efficiently by providing hardware-level isolation between VMs.
VT-x and AMD-V are enabled in the BIOS or UEFI settings. On some systems they are disabled by default. Without hardware virtualization support enabled, VMs either will not run or will run in a slow software emulation mode.
SLAT â€” Second Level Address Translation â€” is an additional CPU feature that improves memory performance in virtual environments. Intel calls it EPT â€” Extended Page Tables. AMD calls it RVI â€” Rapid Virtualization Indexing. SLAT reduces the overhead involved in translating guest virtual addresses to host physical addresses.
---
exam_tips: Type 1 = no host OS, bare metal, enterprise. Type 2 = runs on host OS, workstation/dev. This is a direct exam question â€” know the distinction.

sections.title: Virtualization Use Cases
sections.content:
SANDBOXING.
A VM is an isolated execution environment. Code running inside a VM cannot affect the host system or other VMs. Security professionals use sandboxed VMs to analyze malware â€” running suspicious files in a controlled environment and observing their behavior. After analysis, the VM is discarded or restored from a clean snapshot. The host is unaffected.
Sandboxing is also used for testing software updates, configuration changes, or untrusted scripts before applying them to production systems.
LEGACY SOFTWARE SUPPORT.
Some business-critical applications require an operating system version that cannot be installed on modern hardware, or that cannot be certified compatible with newer OS versions. Running the legacy OS as a VM on modern hardware preserves the application's functionality without maintaining aging physical equipment. A Windows XP VM can run the legacy application while the physical hardware runs a current hypervisor.
CROSS-PLATFORM TESTING.
Developers and QA teams use VMs to run multiple operating systems on a single workstation. Testing a web application across Windows, Linux, and macOS simultaneously requires three VMs rather than three separate computers. Snapshots allow quick rollback to a known-good state before each test run.
TRAINING AND LABS.
VMs are ideal for hands-on IT training. Students can practice configurations, simulate failures, and attempt recovery procedures in an environment where mistakes have no consequences. Restoring a snapshot resets the VM to a clean state in seconds. Lab environments for certifications â€” including A+ labs â€” frequently use VMs for this reason.
SERVER VIRTUALIZATION AND CONSOLIDATION.
Multiple server workloads that previously required separate physical servers can run as VMs on a single host. A physical server running at 5% utilization for a single service is wasteful. Consolidating twenty such services onto a single powerful host improves hardware utilization, reduces power and cooling costs, and simplifies hardware management.
VDI â€” VIRTUAL DESKTOP INFRASTRUCTURE.
VDI hosts virtual desktops on centralized servers. Users connect from thin clients â€” lightweight endpoint devices with no local processing capability â€” to their virtual desktop, which runs on the server.
VDI advantages: desktop images are managed and updated centrally. All user data resides on the server â€” simplified backup. Security policies apply consistently across all virtual desktops. Thin client hardware is cheap and has a long lifespan.
VDI disadvantage: if the network or server fails, users lose access to their desktops. No local processing occurs â€” the endpoint requires continuous server and network connectivity.
APPLICATION VIRTUALIZATION.
Applications are packaged and delivered from a central server. Users launch the application, but the execution occurs on the server â€” not the local device. No local installation is required. Updates are applied once on the server and immediately take effect for all users. Conflicting application versions can coexist on separate servers.
CONTAINERS.
Containers take a fundamentally different approach to isolation. Rather than virtualizing hardware through a hypervisor, containers isolate processes at the operating system level. Multiple containers share the same host OS kernel.
Container characteristics:
Lighter than VMs â€” no guest OS instance required.
Faster startup â€” containers start in seconds compared to minutes for a full VM.
Fewer resources â€” containers share the host kernel and system libraries.
Limitation: containers cannot run a different operating system kernel than the host. A Linux host can run Linux containers. A Windows VM can run any OS.
Containers are used for application deployment, microservices architecture, and lightweight development environments. Docker is the primary container platform.
---
exam_tips: Containers share the host OS kernel â€” they cannot run a different OS. VMs can run any OS. Containers are lighter and faster but less isolated than VMs.

sections.title: Virtualization Resources And Security
sections.content:
RESOURCE REQUIREMENTS.
CPU: hardware virtualization extensions (VT-x / AMD-V) must be enabled. More physical cores directly benefit VM performance â€” VMs compete for CPU time. A host with two cores running four VMs will have all four VMs competing for those two cores simultaneously. SLAT reduces hypervisor CPU overhead for memory access.
RAM: RAM is almost always the primary limiting factor. Each VM requires a dedicated memory allocation â€” whatever is configured, that memory is reserved from the physical pool. The host OS on a Type 2 system also requires RAM. A system running three VMs at 4 GB each plus a host OS needs a minimum of 16 GB of physical RAM â€” realistically more, since the OS and hypervisor also consume memory for their own overhead.
Storage: each VM stores its state in a virtual disk image file. Dynamically expanding images start small and grow as data is added â€” more efficient for initial deployment. Fixed-size images allocate all space immediately â€” more predictable performance. Snapshots preserve the state of a VM at a point in time. Each snapshot requires additional storage space. Large snapshot chains can consume significant disk capacity.
Networking: the hypervisor creates virtual network switches. VMs connect to these virtual switches as if they were connecting to physical switches. Network modes:
Bridged â€” VM gets its own IP address on the physical network, appearing as a separate device.
NAT â€” VM shares the host's IP address, with traffic translated by the hypervisor.
Host-only â€” VM can communicate only with the host and other VMs in the same host-only network.
SECURITY.
Guest OS security: each guest OS requires independent security management. Patching, antivirus, and configuration hardening must be applied to each VM separately. The host system's security tools cannot inspect the internals of guest VMs.
VM sprawl: uncontrolled creation of VMs leads to abandoned, unpatched, unmonitored VMs that become security vulnerabilities. Implement VM lifecycle policies: track all VMs, audit regularly, decommission VMs that are no longer needed.
Host as single point of failure: if the physical host fails, all VMs running on it fail simultaneously. Mitigations: high availability clustering â€” hosts monitor each other and automatically migrate VMs from a failed host to a surviving one. Redundant power supplies and UPS protection for the host. Regular VM backups stored off-host.
VM escape: the most severe virtualization-specific security threat. A VM escape vulnerability allows malicious code executing inside a guest VM to break out of the hypervisor's isolation layer and gain access to the host system or other VMs. If a VM escape is successful, the attacker has compromised not just one VM but the entire host and all VMs running on it. Hypervisor software must be patched promptly when escape vulnerabilities are disclosed.
---
exam_tips: VM escape is the most critical virtualization-specific security threat â€” malicious code in a guest VM gains access to the host or other VMs. Hypervisors must be patched regularly to prevent known escape vulnerabilities.

concept_cards.hook: A Type 1 hypervisor has no host OS underneath it. It IS the operating system for the hardware. A Type 2 hypervisor is an application running inside a regular OS. That distinction determines performance, use case, and where you encounter each.
concept_cards.summary: Virtualization allows multiple operating systems to run simultaneously on a single physical machine. The physical machine is the host.

concept_cards.hook: A VM running a suspicious file has no path to your actual system. When the analysis is done, you snapshot-restore or delete the VM. The malware is gone. The host is untouched. That is sandboxing.
concept_cards.summary: Virtualization serves several distinct use cases beyond simple server consolidation. Sandboxing: a VM is an isolated environment â€” code running inside it cannot affect the host or other VMs.

concept_cards.hook: VM escape is not a software bug you patch and move on from â€” it is a category of vulnerability that lets a guest OS reach across the hypervisor and access the host or other guests. If the hypervisor is compromised, every VM on the host is compromised.
concept_cards.summary: Virtualization resource requirements: CPU: hardware virtualization extensions must be enabled â€” Intel VT-x or AMD-V. Multiple cores improve VM performance significantly because VMs compete for CPU time.

practice_questions.q: What cloud deployment model is used exclusively by a single organization?
What is "elasticity" in cloud computing?
options: Physical flexibility of cloud server hardware
Cost reduction over time through usage
Ability to automatically scale resources up or down based on demand

practice_questions.q: What is the MAIN advantage of cloud-based file storage such as OneDrive or Google Drive for end users?
options: Access files from any device with automatic backup and synchronization
Faster local file access compared to local drives
Better security than all local storage options

practice_questions.q: What does "multi-tenancy" mean in cloud computing?
options: Multiple data centers in different regions
Multiple customers sharing the same physical infrastructure
Multiple administrators managing one cloud account

practice_questions.q: What is the MAIN concern with storing sensitive data in a public cloud environment?
options: Data privacy, compliance requirements, and shared infrastructure security risks
Slower access speeds compared to local storage
Higher cost than all on-premises options

practice_questions.q: Which of the following is an example of SaaS?
What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network) used for?
options: Distributing content geographically closer to users to reduce latency

practice_questions.q: What does "cloud bursting" refer to?
options: Migrating all workloads to the cloud permanently
Automatically offloading excess workloads to the public cloud when on-premises capacity is exceeded

practice_questions.q: What is the purpose of a cloud access security broker (CASB)?
options: Manage cloud billing and cost allocation
Enforce security policies between cloud users and cloud service providers

practice_questions.q: Which term describes the process of moving applications and data from on-premises to a cloud environment?
A small business wants to use cloud software without managing any servers or platforms. Which model is BEST?
What is the primary benefit of using a cloud provider managed database service?
options: Lower cost than any on-premises option
The provider handles patching, backups, scaling, and availability automatically

practice_questions.q: Which hypervisor type installs directly on the physical hardware with no host operating system underneath it?
practice_questions.explanation: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor installs directly on physical hardware — there is no host OS. It boots directly into the hypervisor. Examples include VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V Server, KVM, and Xen. This gives lower overhead and better performance than Type 2, making it suitable for production data centers.

practice_questions.q: A security researcher needs to run a suspicious executable in an isolated environment where it cannot affect the host system. Which virtualization capability is being used?
practice_questions.explanation: Sandboxing uses a VM as an isolated execution environment. Code running inside cannot affect the host or other VMs. After analysis the VM can be discarded or restored from a clean snapshot. This is the standard technique for malware analysis.

practice_questions.q: Which virtualization-specific security threat allows malicious code inside a guest VM to break out of the hypervisor and gain access to the host system?
practice_questions.explanation: VM escape is the most severe virtualization-specific security threat. It allows malicious code in a guest VM to breach the hypervisor isolation layer and access the host system or other VMs. A successful VM escape compromises not just one VM but the entire host. Hypervisors must be patched promptly when escape vulnerabilities are disclosed.

practice_questions.q: What is a virtual machine (VM) snapshot, and what is its primary use?
options: A compressed backup of all VM data stored to tape for long-term archiving
A saved state of a virtual machine at a specific point in time — allows reverting the VM to that state if an update, change, or test causes problems
A real-time clone of a VM running on a separate host for failover
A read-only copy of a VM's disk visible to all VMs in the cluster
practice_questions.explanation: A VM snapshot captures the exact state of a VM (memory, disk, settings) at a moment in time. If a subsequent change (patch, configuration update, malware infection) causes problems, the VM can be instantly reverted to the snapshot state. Snapshots are not substitutes for backups — they are delta files that grow over time.

practice_questions.q: What is live migration in virtualization (e.g., VMware vMotion, Hyper-V Live Migration)?
options: Copying a VM disk image from one storage volume to another while the VM is powered off
Moving a running VM from one physical host to another with zero downtime — workloads continue without interruption
Migrating a VM from on-premises to a cloud provider
Cloning a VM to create an identical replica for load testing
practice_questions.explanation: Live migration transfers a running VM between physical hosts without shutting it down. The hypervisor copies memory pages to the destination host while the VM runs, then switches execution in milliseconds. This enables hardware maintenance, load balancing, and failover without application downtime.

practice_questions.q: What is a virtual switch (vSwitch) in a hypervisor environment?
options: A physical network switch managed by the hypervisor's management software
A software-defined switch within the hypervisor that connects VMs to each other and to physical network adapters, enabling network segmentation and controlled inter-VM communication
A switch that runs as a guest VM alongside other workload VMs
A dedicated physical switch used exclusively for VM storage traffic (iSCSI/NFS)
practice_questions.explanation: A virtual switch is implemented in hypervisor software (VMware vSwitch, Hyper-V Virtual Switch, Linux Bridge). It forwards traffic between VMs and connects VMs to physical NICs. VLANs, QoS, and security policies can be applied at the vSwitch level, controlling VM network behavior centrally.

practice_questions.q: What is thin provisioning in virtual machine storage?
options: Allocating the minimum physical server resources to non-critical VMs

Allocating disk space to VMs on-demand as data is written rather than pre-allocating the full capacity up front — allows overcommitting storage but risks exhausting disk if all VMs grow to their maximum
Compressing VM disk images to reduce storage consumption
A storage type that uses only SSDs for the VM's OS disk while HDDs hold data disks
practice_questions.explanation: With thin provisioning, a 100 GB virtual disk actually only consumes the space currently written to it (e.g., 20 GB). This allows a datastore to host more VMs than physical capacity would nominally allow. The risk is that if all VMs grow simultaneously, the datastore runs out of space, causing all VMs to pause.

practice_questions.q: What is the purpose of vCPU overcommitment in a hypervisor environment?
options: Running a single vCPU at twice its normal clock frequency for workloads that demand it
Assigning more virtual CPUs across VMs than physical CPU cores exist on the host — works because VMs rarely all use 100% CPU simultaneously, improving hardware utilization
Using multiple physical CPUs in a single VM for workloads requiring extreme CPU performance
Limiting the maximum number of vCPUs any single VM can be assigned to prevent monopolization
practice_questions.explanation: vCPU overcommitment is the practice of assigning more vCPUs in total than physical cores. In typical environments, VMs average 20-40% CPU utilization, so a host with 16 physical cores can comfortably run VMs assigned a total of 32-64 vCPUs. The hypervisor schedules vCPU execution across physical cores dynamically.
